strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-motivated: the computational asymmetry between embarrassingly parallel inference and synchronization-heavy policy updates is a real and timely problem in RL for LLM reasoning.

The core idea (generate more rollouts than are used for the gradient update, and select an informative subset) is simple, framework-agnostic, and easy to implement; the framing as a down-sampling rule (Definition 3.1) is clean.

Lemma 3.1 provides a neat exact characterization of the variance-maximizing subset (k highest plus m−k lowest rewards), and the O(n log n + m²) algorithm makes the method practical at negligible overhead.
The experimental protocol is more careful than typical: 8 random seeds per algorithm, 5 evaluations per checkpoint, and standard error bands reported in Figure 1.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is very thin for the central claims. Only one benchmark (GSM8K), one model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with LoRA), and one (n, m) configuration (32→16) are tested. The paper introduces two alternative down-sampling rules (random and max-reward) as baselines but never evaluates either — a critical omission.

Without a random down-sampling control (GRPO-PODS with Drand, which the authors themselves note is 'equivalent to standard GRPO with m rollouts'), it is impossible to attribute the observed gains to the max-variance selection rule rather than simply to doubling the number of rollouts (n=32 vs n=16). This control would have been nearly free to run, and its absence is the decisive evidential gap.

The claimed resource-efficiency motivation (memory and communication bottlenecks in the update phase) is never measured: there are no wall-clock breakdowns, throughput numbers, memory profiles, or scalability results. The experiments compare performance vs. training time on a single A6000, which does not directly substantiate the distributed-systems motivation in Section 1 and the abstract.

The proof of Lemma 3.1 contains a gap: the assertion that a non-extreme optimal subset must contain an element of type (i) or (ii) is stated but not rigorously established (the case analysis for elements below/above the mean is incomplete as written). The result is plausible and likely known in essence, but the proof as presented is not airtight; the tightness of the O(n log n + m²) bound also relies on it.

Systematic bias of the selection rule is not analyzed. Max-variance down-sampling deterministically retains the most extreme rewards, discarding medium-quality rollouts; this shifts the effective on-policy distribution and interacts with advantage normalization over the selected subset (a_S,i uses μS, σS of the selected subset). Potential pathologies (e.g., on problems where all rollouts succeed or fail, or degradation of the policy's calibrated exploration) are neither theorized about nor tested. The connection to DAPO's dynamic sampling is mentioned but not empirically compared.

The improvement in Figure 1 is roughly 1% accuracy with partially overlapping error bands in places; no statistical significance tests are reported, and the claimed 'consistent' separation would benefit from quantitative support.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, and key details (prompt template, prompts per step, batch size during updates, evaluation protocol, how the holdout set relates to the official GSM8K test split) are missing. There is no limitations section discussing the narrow scope of evaluation or the bias concerns above.

The theoretical contribution, while tidy, is modest: the exchange-argument result is essentially folklore-level, and the 'information-theoretically motivated' framing of max-variance selection is asserted (via citation [35]) rather than derived for this setting.

strengths: The core idea—decoupling the embarrassingly parallel inference phase from the memory/communication-bound update phase by training on a selected subset of rollouts—is simple, sensible, and addresses a real practical concern in RL for LLMs.

Lemma 3.1 and Algorithm 2 provide a clean, correct-in-spirit result showing the variance-maximizing subset consists of extreme rewards, making the selection rule practical; the proof structure (exchange argument) is reasonable.

The evaluation methodology is careful in one respect: the comparison is against standard GRPO under equal wall-clock training time on the same hardware, with 8 random seeds and repeated evaluations, which is the fair operational comparison for the claimed efficiency benefit.

The paper is clearly written, the PODS framework is stated precisely (Definition 3.1, Algorithm 1), and hyperparameters are reported in enough detail to be reproducible; related work adequately positions the method against DAPO and VAPO.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is too narrow to support the paper's central claim. The evaluation covers only GSM8K, one model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct), LoRA fine-tuning, and a single (n=32, m=16) configuration. For a paper whose motivating claim spans 'a wide range of hardware environments,' no scaling study over n/m ratios, model sizes, or other benchmarks (e.g., MATH) is provided.

A decisive ablation is missing: standard GRPO with n=32 rollouts updating on all 32. Without it, the paper cannot distinguish whether gains come from the down-sampling/selection rule or merely from having 32 candidate rollouts available. This gap directly undermines the title claim that 'not all rollouts are useful.'

The paper introduces two baseline strategies—random down-sampling and max-reward down-sampling—but never evaluates them. The comparison in Fig. 1 only includes max-variance selection, so there is no evidence that max-variance is the right selection criterion, which is the paper's main methodological contribution.

The measured improvement is small (~1 percentage point) and the confidence bands of GRPO-PODS and GRPO substantially overlap across much of the training trajectory; no statistical significance test is reported, so the claim of 'consistently outperforms' and 'clearly improves' is overstated.

The theoretical contribution is minor. The fact that a variance-maximizing subset of sorted scalars consists of extremes is folklore-adjacent and closely related to classical results in the data-selection/coreset literature the paper itself cites; moreover, the proof of Lemma 3.1 contains a gap—the step claiming (r_{i-1}-r_i)[(r_{i-1}+r_i)-(mu'+mu)] >= 0 requires an argument that r_{i-1}+r_i <= mu'+mu that is asserted but not rigorously established.

Potential degeneracies of the method are unexamined. With rule-based binary rewards, the variance-maximizing subset may contain only all-correct or all-incorrect rollouts within a group, yielding near-zero group-relative advantages and wasted gradient steps; the interaction between selection and GRPO's group normalization is not analyzed.

The computational-asymmetry motivation is asserted but never quantified. No profiling or measurement of actual inference vs. update time/memory on the testbed is provided, so the claimed practical benefit is not demonstrated beyond the single wall-clock curve.

The novelty claim ('first to apply down-sampling and data selection techniques to the rollout generation process') is thin given the close relationship to prioritized experience replay [27-29] and DAPO's dynamic sampling [18]; the conceptual delta over these works is modest.
No code release or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, and there is no limitations section discussing the narrow scope of evaluation.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the core idea—decoupling the embarrassingly parallel inference phase from the communication- and memory-bound update phase by training on an informative rollout subset—is intuitive and well-motivated.

Lemma 3.1 and its proof are essentially correct and give a clean, efficient algorithm (Theorem 1, O(n log n + m^2)) for the variance-maximizing subset selection; the extremal structure also gives an appealing interpretation in terms of contrastive positive/negative signals.

The empirical protocol is reasonably careful: 8 independent seeds, 5 evaluations per checkpoint, standard-error shading in Figure 1, and comparison along the wall-clock training-time axis on a single A6000.
The related work discussion is honest about the similarity to DAPO's dynamic sampling and VAPO's rollout-scaling, and positions the contribution as complementary.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is confounded by an unfair baseline design. GRPO-PODS uses n=32 rollouts per prompt while the GRPO baseline uses n=16, i.e., PODS consumes twice the inference compute (and reward-model evaluations). The paper's own thesis is that inference is cheap, but the reported gain could simply reflect having 32 samples per prompt rather than the max-variance selection rule itself. The decisive missing ablations are: (a) standard GRPO with n=32 using all rollouts, and (b) GRPO-PODS with random down-sampling (D_rand) and max-reward down-sampling (D_maxr)—both of which are defined in Section 3.2 but never evaluated. Without these, the paper cannot support its claim that max-variance selection drives the improvement.

The evaluation is very narrow: a single benchmark (GSM8K), a single model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) with LoRA at rank 64, and a single (n, m) setting. GSM8K is an easy benchmark where a 3B instruct model is already at ~80%; there is no evidence on harder math (e.g., MATH), code, or long-CoT settings where the claimed efficiency asymmetry would matter most, and no study of how performance varies with the m/n ratio.

The effect size in Figure 1 is modest (~1 point) with visibly overlapping error bands in the early and middle portions of training; the text claims 'consistently outperforms' but no statistical significance testing is reported for the endpoint gap.

There is no theoretical or empirical analysis of the bias introduced by reward-dependent subset selection. Selecting S as a function of r and then computing advantages only within S changes the expectation of the policy-gradient estimator; the paper does not discuss whether this biases learning (e.g., toward problems with bimodal reward distributions) or whether it causes distributional pathologies over training.

The characterization of max-variance selection as 'information-theoretically motivated' is not substantiated by any information-theoretic analysis; the motivating connection to [35] is asserted rather than established. The lemma itself is a folklore extremal fact (extreme values maximize variance), which limits the technical novelty.

Reproducibility support is thin: no code release, no mention of which GRPO implementation was used, no hyperparameter search details, and no limitations section discussing generalization or the selection-bias concern above.

Minor: the claim of being 'the first' to apply data selection to rollouts is stated strongly given closely related filtering ideas in DAPO [18] and experience-replay prioritization lines of work [27–29].

strengths: The paper addresses a real and timely systems-level problem in RLVR training: the computational asymmetry between embarrassingly parallel rollout generation and communication-heavy policy updates. The proposed solution (generate many rollouts, train on a subset) is simple, well-motivated, and practically deployable.

The max-variance down-sampling rule comes with a correctness proof and an O(n log n) algorithm (Lemma 3.1, Theorem 1), plus a clean binary-reward special case (Theorem 2), so the selection rule is not merely heuristic and is cheap to compute.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough for the scale considered: three settings spanning single-GPU LoRA and 8xH100 distributed training, comparisons against both standard GRPO and gradient-accumulation GRPO, and ablations over (n, m) and three down-sampling rules (Figs. 2-4). Plots use wall-clock time on the x-axis with standard-error bands, which is the right basis for an efficiency claim, and setting (c) holds total rollouts constant (512 per prompt) to isolate the effect of down-sampling.

The limitations section is honest and substantive: it correctly identifies that PODS makes training off-policy by altering the rollout distribution, that gains may not transfer to non-verifiable-reward domains, and that a prompt-diversity alternative exists. The broader-impact discussion is adequate.
The work is orthogonal to existing methods (DAPO, VAPO) and the related-work section clearly delineates the distinction (systematic down-sampling of the rollout pool).
weaknesses: The scale and scope of evaluation is modest for the central claims: only Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, only GSM8K and MATH, short training runs (6 hours or 30 minutes). There is no evidence the gains persist at larger model scale, on harder benchmarks (e.g., AIME, competition-level MATH), or in longer-horizon RLVR training where selection-induced distribution shift could compound. Claims like 'consistently outperforms' rest on relatively small margins (e.g., ~1-2 points in Fig. 2b).

The theoretical contribution is elementary. Lemma 3.1 (the variance-maximizing subset consists of extremes) is close to folklore, and the swap-based proof is not fully rigorous as written: in case (i), the step asserting Var(S') - Var(S*) >= 0 from (r_{i-1} - r_i)[(r_{i-1}+r_i) - (mu' + mu)] >= 0 requires justification of the sign of the second factor, which depends on mu' and is only asserted. The argument also needs a termination/measure argument to show the repeated-swap procedure reaches the claimed form.

The estimator bias introduced by re-normalizing advantages on the selected subset (mu_S, sigma_S) is not analyzed. Max-variance selection systematically produces high-variance, bimodal reward subsets, which inflates normalized advantage magnitudes relative to the full pool; the paper does not disentangle whether gains come from 'informative selection' or simply from larger advantage magnitudes, nor does it quantify the off-policy bias acknowledged in limitations.

Comparison fairness is uneven across settings: in settings (a) and (b), GRPO-PODS generates 4x more rollouts per step than the GRPO baseline (n=64 vs 16), shifting cost from update to inference; only setting (c) holds total rollouts constant. The claimed 'superior performance over standard GRPO' would be more convincing with a matched-inference-compute baseline (e.g., more prompts with fewer rollouts), which the authors themselves note in limitations but do not test.

Key baselines are missing from the rule comparison: only max-variance, max-reward, and random rules are compared (Fig. 4). Rules closer to the advantage structure (e.g., variance-preserving stratified sampling, or DAPO-style dynamic filtering which is cited as similar) would better establish that variance maximization is the operative factor.

Reproducibility is undermined by an incomplete artifact: the code availability statement reads 'We publish the code for our experiments at .' with the URL missing. The number of seeds/runs per configuration is also never stated explicitly, so the standard-error bands cannot be fully interpreted, and no significance tests are reported.

Some narrative claims outrun the evidence, e.g., the introduction asserts that extra rollouts 'introduce noise into the training that can degrade the converging performance,' but this is never demonstrated directly; Fig. 3a's dip at n=256 is attributed partly to per-step runtime, which is a throughput effect rather than a learning-signal effect.

strengths: The paper identifies a real practical bottleneck in RLVR training (the asymmetry between embarrassingly parallel inference and communication-heavy policy updates) and proposes a simple, deployable fix that is easy to implement within existing GRPO pipelines.

The core theoretical result is clean: Lemma 3.1 shows variance-maximizing subsets consist of extreme-reward rollouts, and Algorithm 2 with prefix sums yields an O(n log n) solution; Theorem 2 gives an interpretable closed form for binary rewards (m/2 highest + m/2 lowest).
Ablations are reasonably thorough: the paper varies rollout size n, update size m, and compares three down-sampling rules, and reports per-step wall-clock timings alongside accuracy.

The limitations section is honest, correctly noting that PODS introduces off-policy behavior, that gains may not transfer beyond math reasoning with verifiable rewards, and that prompt-diversity alternatives exist.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The central idea—generating more rollouts than are used for the update and filtering them—closely overlaps with existing practice. DAPO's dynamic sampling already discards non-informative rollouts, and filtering zero-variance groups is common in GRPO implementations. The claim of being 'the first to apply principled down-sampling to the rollout-generation stage' (Section 2) is overstated; the genuinely new content is the variance-maximization criterion, and in the binary-reward case it reduces to the obvious strategy of training on equal numbers of successes and failures.

The key empirical claim that max-variance selection matters is weakly supported. In Fig. 4, random down-sampling performs nearly on par with max-variance for most of training, so the advantage of the theoretically motivated rule over trivial baselines appears small. The binary-reward case (GSM8K/MATH with rule-based correctness rewards) means the sophisticated O(n log n) machinery essentially implements 'pick m/2 correct and m/2 incorrect', which practitioners already do.

The efficiency argument is setting-dependent and the comparisons are not fully controlled. PODS uses 4x more inference compute (n=64 vs n=16); the reported gains hold in regimes where generation is cheap relative to updates, but on many multi-GPU setups generation is the bottleneck, in which case PODS wastes compute. This asymmetry is acknowledged only obliquely in the limitations.

Statistical rigor is unclear. The shaded areas are 1.96 standard errors, but the number of seeds/runs is never stated. The GSM8K improvement (~1-2%) is within or near the overlapping confidence bands in Fig. 2a, so the headline claim of consistent superiority is not convincingly established.

The evaluation is narrow: only a 3B model on GSM8K and MATH, with no code-generation or harder reasoning benchmarks (e.g., AIME), and no comparison against the closest related method (DAPO's over-sampling-and-filter) that would isolate the contribution.

The advantage re-normalization on the selected subset (a_{S,i} using mu_S, sigma_S) introduces a biased, off-policy estimator whose effect is not analyzed or ablated separately from the selection rule itself.

The theoretical framing is inflated. The criterion is called 'information-theoretically motivated' and justified by appeal to Razin et al., but no information-theoretic argument is actually made; Theorem 2 is trivial, and the proof of Lemma 3.1, while essentially correct, glosses over edge cases in the swap argument.

Reproducibility concerns: the code release statement is incomplete ('We publish the code for our experiments at .' with no URL), and several important details (number of seeds, test-set sizes, evaluation protocol, training data sizes) are missing.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated systems issue in RLVR training: the computational asymmetry between embarrassingly parallel rollout generation and communication-heavy policy updates. Framing the fix as down-sampling rather than more memory-saving tricks is a clean and practical idea.

The theoretical contribution, while elementary, is correct and useful: Lemma 3.1 shows the variance-maximizing subset consists of extreme rewards, Algorithm 2 achieves O(n log n), and Theorem 2 gives the intuitive binary-reward special case (m/2 highest + m/2 lowest). The proof sketch of the swap argument checks out under the stated case conditions.

The experimental design in setting (c) is commendably careful: total rollouts (512) are held constant across GRPO-GA and GRPO-PODS, isolating the effect of down-sampling. Ablations over (n, m) and three down-sampling rules (max-variance, max-reward, random) are informative and show the selection rule matters, not merely the smaller update set.

The limitations section is honest and specific: it acknowledges restriction to math RLVR, the off-policy nature of selective down-sampling, and the existence of an alternative path (more prompts, fewer rollouts). A broader impact statement and promised code release are included.
The paper is well written and clearly structured; Figures 1–4 communicate the method and results effectively, including per-step runtime measurements that let readers judge wall-clock trade-offs.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is thin for a main-track paper. The O(n log n) algorithm follows directly from the observation that variance is maximized by picking extremes—a result that many readers will find immediately intuitive, and Theorem 2 is essentially trivial. The novelty over prior art (DAPO's dynamic skipping of zero-variance prompts, over-generation in VAPO, and hard-filtering approaches) is incremental; the related-work comparison with these methods is superficial.

Missing the most natural baseline: simply discarding all-correct/all-wrong groups (or training only on groups with reward variance) before down-sampling, as in DAPO-style dynamic sampling. Since GRPO advantages are already zero for constant-reward groups, the claimed gains over 'standard GRPO' may substantially conflate discarding uninformative prompts with the max-variance selection rule. Comparisons only against max-reward and random rules within PODS do not establish superiority over existing filtering approaches.

The central empirical claim that 'additional samples not only provide diminishing returns but also introduce noise that can degrade converging performance' is asserted without direct evidence. The single-peaked curve in Fig. 3a is explicitly confounded by the per-step runtime increase for large n; no experiment isolates the alleged noise mechanism.

Bias introduced by the method is not analyzed. Selecting extremes and then re-normalizing advantages over the selected subset (µ_S, σ_S) changes the learning signal in ways that could introduce systematic bias; the paper acknowledges off-policy behavior in limitations but provides no theoretical or empirical analysis of the estimator bias, nor a comparison against keeping the full-group advantage normalization while subsetting the update.

Scale and generality of evaluation are limited: a single 3B model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct), two math benchmarks, and short training runs (≤6 hours single-GPU; 30 minutes multi-GPU). No comparison against PPO variants or stronger recent pipelines, and the mult-GPU setting compares only against GRPO-GA rather than standard GRPO. The number of seeds underlying the 1.96-SEM shaded regions is never stated, so the reliability of the small accuracy gaps (e.g., ~1–2 points in Fig. 2a) is unclear.

The code-release statement is incomplete (the URL is blank: 'We publish the code for our experiments at .'), which undermines the reproducibility claim. Additionally, Theorem 2 is stated only for even m without discussion of the odd-m case, and several details (e.g., exact reward-format functions, evaluation protocol, test-set sizes) are deferred or unspecified.
